questions_asked: At a busy airport security checkpoint, which single step causes passengers to wait longest and pile up most: the ID-check counter, the X-ray belt, or the millimeter-wave body scanner?

You said the X-ray belt is the main bottleneck because bags pass one at a time through the machine and an officer reviews the image. What stops a single X-ray belt from processing bags much faster — is it the belt's physical speed, the officer reviewing images, or something else?
You said the officer's decision on each bag's X-ray image is what caps the belt. For a normal, unflagged bag, roughly how many seconds does that officer take per image on average?
At a typical US airport checkpoint on a normal day, what fraction of bags get flagged for a secondary hand search by the officer — roughly what percent?
When a passenger walks through the millimeter-wave body scanner, what fraction get stopped for a pat-down by an officer, on a normal day?
At a regular (non-Pre-Check) lane, how long does a passenger typically take to remove shoes, jacket, belt, electronics and liquids into bins, then put everything back after the scan?

You said divesting is faster for experienced travelers and slower for families or infrequent flyers. How much slower, roughly, does a first-time or family traveler take to divest compared to a frequent flyer?

In a security queue, some cultures strictly hold their place in line while others are more willing to squeeze in or let a friend join ahead. How does that tendency to let people cut in affect the smoothness of a queue?

The problem says about 45% of US passengers enroll in Pre-Check, but only one Pre-Check lane is open for every three regular lanes. On a normal busy day, is the Pre-Check line usually shorter or longer than a regular line?
At the first ID-check counter where an officer verifies a passenger's ID and boarding pass, how long does one officer typically spend per passenger on a busy day?
expert_answers:
The X-ray belt is the dominant bottleneck.

Reason: it is the only step where every passenger's throughput is gated by a shared, serial resource — the conveyor and the single X-ray image reviewer — and where each passenger's service time is inflated by divesting and reclaiming multiple bins (shoes, jackets, electronics, liquids, laptops). Divesting/reclaiming alone typically takes tens of seconds per passenger, and flagged bags add unpredictable extra service. ID check is fast (a few seconds per passenger) and easily parallelized by adding officers; the body scanner is also short (a few seconds) and parallelizable by adding lanes. The X-ray belt, by contrast, has a hard mechanical throughput ceiling and long, variable per-passenger occupancy, so queues and variance concentrate there.

This is an empirical judgment based on typical checkpoint service times, not a computed result.

The binding constraint is usually the human image reviewer, not the belt's physical speed.

The belt itself moves at a fixed, modest speed (roughly 0.2–0.3 m/s), but that only sets a floor on spacing between bags. The real limit is that each bag's image must be visually interpreted by a screening officer, who must decide clear/flag, and who can only attend to one image stream at a time. That decision time — a few seconds per bag, longer for cluttered or flagged bags — is what caps throughput, and it is why one belt cannot simply be sped up to process more bags.

Secondary factors: bags must be spaced so images don't overlap, and divesting/reclaiming at the belt ends creates gaps and surges. But if you removed the reviewer constraint, the belt speed and spacing alone would allow considerably higher throughput.

This is an empirical judgment, not a computed result.

Roughly 3–6 seconds per normal, unflagged bag image — an empirical judgment, not a measured figure.

That covers the officer's glance, pattern recognition, and clear/flag decision, plus the small handling gap between consecutive images. It is the same order as the belt's own spacing floor, which is why the reviewer, not belt speed, sets the ceiling. Cluttered or flagged bags take noticeably longer (often 10–30+ seconds once a secondary search is involved), which is what drives the variance.

Roughly 5–15% of bags get flagged for secondary hand search on a normal day — an empirical judgment, not a measured figure.

Most bags clear on the image alone; flags come from cluttered/overlapping images, ambiguous items, and random or alarm-triggered selections. The rate rises with passenger volume, bag clutter, and tightened security posture, and can spike well above this range on high-alert days.

Roughly 2–5% of passengers get stopped for a pat-down on a normal day — an empirical judgment, not a measured figure.

Most passengers clear the scanner or metal detector on the first pass. Pat-downs are triggered by alarms (metal, anomalies), random selection, and opt-outs, and the rate rises with tightened security posture or higher alarm sensitivity.

Roughly 30–60 seconds total for a typical regular-lane passenger — an empirical judgment, not a measured figure.

That splits into two parts: divesting (removing shoes, belt, jacket, emptying pockets, pulling out laptop and liquids, loading bins) typically takes about 20–40 seconds, and reclaiming (collecting bins, re-dressing, repacking) about 10–20 seconds. It is faster for experienced travelers and slower for families, infrequent flyers, and those with many items. Pre-Check passengers skip shoes, belt, jacket, and laptop removal, cutting this to roughly half.

Roughly 2–3× slower — an empirical judgment, not a measured figure.

A frequent flyer who knows the routine divests in about 15–25 seconds. A first-time or family traveler typically takes 45–90+ seconds, because of unfamiliarity with the rules, multiple people and bags to manage, children needing help, and repeated trips to the bin. Families with young children or groups with many items can exceed that, and the spread (variance) is much wider than the mean difference.

Letting people cut in degrades queue smoothness, mainly by breaking the first-come-first-served discipline that keeps a single-file queue orderly.

Effects:
- It adds unaccounted arrivals at the front, so the effective service rate seen by waiting passengers drops and their wait times rise unpredictably.
- It creates local congestion and jostling at the merge point, which can physically slow the line and cause gaps upstream.
- It increases variance: whether and when someone cuts is irregular, so wait times become less predictable even at constant throughput.
- It can trigger defensive behavior (people crowding forward, guarding their spot), which further disrupts spacing and flow.

The magnitude depends on how often it happens and whether it is tolerated by those behind. A culture that strictly holds place produces a smoother, more predictable queue; one that tolerates cutting produces a faster-moving but more erratic and less fair-feeling line. This is a qualitative judgment, not a measured result.

Pre-Check is usually shorter — often much shorter — despite the lane ratio.

Reason: Pre-Check passengers move faster at every step (no shoe/belt/jacket/laptop removal, so divesting and reclaiming are roughly halved), so each open Pre-Check lane has both a higher service rate and a lower per-passenger service time. With 45% of passengers spread over one lane for every three regular lanes, the Pre-Check lane carries about 45/25 ≈ 1.8× the passenger volume of a regular lane, but its throughput per lane is also higher, so the queue is typically shorter and less variable.

Caveat: this holds on normal days. Because there are so few Pre-Check lanes, a surge or a single slow/flagged passenger can make the Pre-Check line spike sharply, so its wait is shorter on average but can be less predictable. This is an empirical judgment, not a computed result.

Roughly 5–15 seconds per passenger on a busy day — an empirical judgment, not a measured figure.

That covers the officer taking the ID and boarding pass, glancing at the photo and name, matching them to the passenger, and waving them through. It is fast and fairly consistent, which is why ID check rarely becomes the bottleneck: it is easily parallelized by opening more counters, and its service time is short and low-variance compared with divesting/reclaiming at the X-ray belt. Longer times occur mainly for flagged documents, secondary verification, or confused passengers, but those are a small minority.
